newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal politicians jostle to form new government.
newsitem.headline: Nepal politicians jostle to form new government.

text.p: Nepal was in the grip of political uncertainty on Saturday as politicians jostled to form the Himalayan kingdom's fourth government in six years.
Major political groups were locked in tough bargaining aimed at creating an alternative to the centre-right coalition government which was voted out on Thursday.

King Birendra on Friday set a deadline of March 10 for the country's parties to stake a claim to power after Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba resigned following the defeat of his 17-month-old coalition in a confidence vote.
Deuba's Nepali Congress party said it was ready for a new coalition with the communists if they accepted its leadership.

The opposition Communist Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) Party, which ruled for 10 months until Deuba's coalition took office in September 1995 and controls the largest number of seats in parliament, is demanding the prime ministership, politicians involved in the negotiations told Reuters.
"It is undemocratic for the Nepali Congress to claim leadership in the new coalition since it has already been defeated in the parliament," UML General Secretary Madhav Kumar Nepal said.
Birendra, who made himself a British-style constitutional monarch in November 1990, has called for proposals by 6:00 p.m. (1215 GMT) on Monday for a new government.
Nepal, which maintained self-imposed isolation until the middle of this century, is one of the world's 10 poorest countries. Annual income averages $200 a head.
Political analysts said if the UML and Nepali Congress failed to come together, each would have to turn for support to the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) which holds decisive votes.

The RPP, a key partner in the outgoing coalition, was formed by the former rulers of the panchayat system which was overthrown by the Nepali Congress and the communists during a 1990 pro-democracy movement that estalished multi-party democracy in the world's only Hindu kingdom.

The UML and its allies command 94 members in the 205-member House of Representatives against 87 controlled by the Nepali Congress. The RPP, which has 19 seats, is sharply divided over support for a new government.
"We will present ourselves in the dialogue (with other parties) in a reasonable way in keeping with the ground realities," said RPP president Surya Bahadur Thapa.
The communists said they wanted the new alliance to agree on an agenda that could include fighting corruption, reform in election procedures and reforms in the bureaucracy.
Nepali Congress officials said the party's terms for potential partners included political stability and a code of conduct that would ensure the new government's smooth functioning.
